title: Negative quasiprobability trajectories for Bell-diagonal states under local decoherence
authors: Qing Yu, Kun Zhang, Yang-Yang Chen, Xiao-Hui Wang
abstract: The fluctuation theorem (FT) relates microscopic trajectory distributions to macroscopic averages. Using quasiprobability trajectories, this framework has recently been extended to quantum information dynamics. Despite sharing the form of conventional thermodynamic FTs, information FTs involve quasiprobabilities whose negativity and statistical properties remain poorly understood. We analytically determine the properties of negative distributions based on the two-qubit Bell-diagonal states evolving under local dephasing, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping channels. We show that the occurrence of negative quasiprobabilities is not determined by the entanglement or Bell nonlocality of the initial state. Instead, a diagonal-interference decomposition of the transition quasiprobability provides a sufficient condition for negativity. More importantly, we prove that quasiprobability distributions containing negative weights can violate Horváth's necessary and sufficient criterion for the Jensen-Steffensen inequality to hold for every continuous convex function, even though the specific exponential Jensen-like relation enforced by the FT and the quantum data-processing inequality remains valid. This trajectory-level contrast with classical stochastic descriptions reveals a distinctive feature of quantum information dynamics that is invisible when only the corresponding average-level information inequalities are considered.
summary: This paper analyzes how quantum information changes during local decoherence by examining quasiprobability trajectories. It demonstrates that these distributions can exhibit negative weights, leading to violations of certain mathematical criteria (Horváth's criterion). This highlights a fundamental difference between the full quantum trajectory description and what is observable only through average measurements.
main_problem: The study investigates negative quasiprobability trajectories for Bell-diagonal quantum states undergoing local decoherence, contrasting trajectory-level dynamics with average-level inequalities.
main_result: Negative quasiprobabilities can violate Horváth's criterion for the Jensen-Steffensen inequality to hold, revealing a unique feature of quantum information dynamics invisible when only average quantities are considered.
method: The authors use quasiprobability trajectories (Kirkwood-Dirac distribution) derived from fluctuation theorems applied to quantum mutual information change ($\Delta I$).
model_or_system: The system consists of two qubits initialized in Bell-diagonal states and subjected to local decoherence channels, including dephasing, depolarizing, and amplitude damping.
key_observables: Quantum Mutual Information change ($\Delta I$), stochastic mutual information change ($\Delta\iota[\gamma]$), and the negativity of the quasiprobability distribution $Q[	ilde{\gamma}]$.
important_parameters: Decoherence parameters such as $\lambda$ (dephasing) or $\eta$ (depolarizing noise); the analysis also depends on initial state populations ($p_k$) and environmental coupling strengths ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The use of the Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution is necessary because spectral projectors for global and local states do not commute due to entanglement.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that for initial Bell-diagonal states under dephasing or depolarization, the reduced trajectory weights $Q_S[\gamma]$ remain non-negative relative to the zero line.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the framework using fluctuation theorems and quasiprobabilities. It then analyzes specific decoherence channels (dephasing/depolarizing) showing non-negativity in reduced distributions, before focusing on amplitude damping to analytically determine minimum support values and prove the violation of Horváth's criterion.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, trajectory-level diagnostic tool that distinguishes quantum dynamics from classical stochastic processes, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems beyond simple average measurements.
